changes.new: ### Echoed updates and gradient accumulation With batch echoing, the optimizer updates its parameters and then evaluates the same batch again. Gradient accumulation evaluates several microbatches before the next optimizer update. Even when both procedures use the same examples twice, their second gradient need not be the same. For a scalar parameter, take the loss $L(\theta)=\tfrac12(\theta-1)^2$, whose gradient is $\theta-1$. Start at $\theta_0=0$ and use plain SGD with learning rate $\eta=0.5$. The first echoed update has gradient $-1$ and moves the parameter to $0.5$. The next evaluation of the same example has gradient $-0.5$ and moves it to $0.75$. If two identical microbatches are instead evaluated at the unchanged initial parameter, their mean gradient is still $-1$; one update reaches $0.5$, not $0.75$. ```python def echoed_sgd(initial, learning_rate, presentations): parameter = initial trace = [] for _ in range(presentations): gradient = parameter - 1 parameter -= learning_rate * gradient trace.append((gradient, parameter)) return parameter, trace echoed, trace = echoed_sgd(0., .5, 2) accumulated_mean_gradient = ((0. - 1.) + (0. - 1.)) / 2 accumulated = 0. - .5 * accumulated_mean_gradient assert trace == [(-1., .5), (-.5, .75)] assert echoed == .75 and accumulated == .5 print("echoed updates", trace, "one averaged-gradient update", accumulated) ``` This comparison uses two presentations in both cases, but two optimizer updates for echoing and one for accumulation. Summing instead of averaging the accumulated gradients would change the gradient scale again. With momentum, adaptive optimizer state or a learning-rate schedule, update ordering also changes that state. Echo factor, optimizer-step budget and loss reduction therefore need to be specified separately. Choi and Dahl's [illustrated walkthrough](https://research.google/blog/speeding-up-neural-network-training-with-data-echoing/) shows the original pipeline and idle-time diagrams, and distinguishes example echoing from batch echoing. Echoing before stochastic augmentation can create a new view on each presentation; echoing an already augmented batch reuses that transformed input. Neither arrangement is equivalent to obtaining new independent labelled examples. Choi et al., [Data Echoing, §2 and §3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/1907.05550v3#S2),
